title: Ezra 2:1–35
context: The long list of returnees begins here with the lay houses, after a heading that names those who came up from the captivity Nebuchadnezzar had carried to Babylon, and who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his city, with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other leaders. The list is a record of families and hometowns, not a coded lesson in the names or the figures. A closely parallel list stands in Nehemiah 7:6–73. Many lines agree; others differ in a name, a count, or both, and some families or towns appear in only one of the two. Those differences should be named and left as they stand, without harmonizing and without a theological contrast over a total or a spelling. The assembly figure of forty-two thousand three hundred sixty will be given later, in 2:64, and the numbers in this unit should not be forced to equal it in advance. Both traditions read 2:1–35 as a historical enrollment of the people who came up, and they take the Nehemiah 7 parallels as a second witness to be set beside this one, not as a text to be rewritten into it.

verses.text: Now these are the children of the province who went up out of the captivity of those who had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away to Babylon, and who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, everyone to his city;
verses.arminianNotes:
These are “the children of the province who went up out of the captivity of those who had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away to Babylon, and who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, everyone to his city;” The heading matches the substance of Nehemiah 7:6, with small differences of wording, including the mention of Babylon as the place of exile here.

Arminian readers take the title as a real census of returnees, people of the province going home city by city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a historical heading, the same return described in Nehemiah 7:6, not a symbolic people invented for a later lesson.

Both traditions begin the list as a record of those who actually went up, and they do not force the two titles into one wording.

verses.text: who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verses.arminianNotes:
They came with “Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah.” Eleven leaders are named, then the number of the men of the people of Israel. Nehemiah 7:7 has a similar list with twelve names: Azariah, Raamiah, and Nahamani appear there, Mispereth and Nehum stand where this verse has Mispar and Rehum, and Seraiah and Reelaiah are the names here. Zerubbabel and Jeshua stand first in both. Sheshbazzar was called the prince of Judah in 1:8; whether he is the same man as Zerubbabel is left open, as already noted there.

Arminian readers take the eleven names as the leaders this book records, without merging them into Nehemiah’s twelve.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the two rosters side by side. The extra name and the changed spellings in Nehemiah 7:7 are to be reported, not erased, and Zerubbabel’s relation to Sheshbazzar remains a question, not a conclusion.

Both traditions refuse a contrast over the names and keep the identity question hedged.

verses.text: The children of Parosh, two thousand one hundred seventy-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Parosh number two thousand one hundred seventy-two, the same count as Nehemiah 7:8. The line is a family enrollment in the return, not a symbol in the name or the figure.

Arminian readers take the number as a real count of this house, standing in agreement with the parallel list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a historical figure that matches Nehemiah 7 in this line. The house is named and numbered, and the two books agree here.

Both traditions leave an agreeing count as it stands and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: The children of Arah, seven hundred seventy-five.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Arah number seven hundred seventy-five; Nehemiah 7:10 has six hundred fifty-two. The two lists should be reported side by side, without choosing one figure as if the other were not written.

Arminian readers take this book’s count as the number it actually records, and they refuse to rewrite it from Nehemiah 7.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name both figures and leave them unharmonized. The difference is a matter of the lists, not of doctrine.

Both traditions refuse a theological contrast over the counts and do not invent a single reconstructed total.

verses.text: The children of Pahathmoab, of the children of Jeshua and Joab, two thousand eight hundred twelve.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Pahathmoab, of the children of Jeshua and Joab, number two thousand eight hundred twelve. Nehemiah 7:11 has two thousand eight hundred eighteen for the same house. The two figures should stand together, unharmonized.

Arminian readers take this verse’s count as the number Ezra records, and they do not correct it from the other list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report both totals for Pahathmoab and refuse to treat the difference as a doctrinal issue.

Both traditions leave the two counts as they are written and invent no contrast over them.

verses.text: The children of Bani, six hundred forty-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Bani number six hundred forty-two. Nehemiah 7:15 has the children of Binnui, six hundred forty-eight, a different name and a different count. The notes record the difference of name and, where it exists, of number, without forcing one reading.

Arminian readers keep this verse’s wording and refuse to substitute the parallel name as if it had been written here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the two lines side by side. A changed name, and in some cases a changed count, is to be named and left open.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spelling or the figure, and they do not merge the lists.

verses.text: The children of Ater, of Hezekiah, ninety-eight.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Ater, of Hezekiah, number ninety-eight, the same count as Nehemiah 7:21, which also names Ater of Hezekiah. The family is distinguished by that further name, and the two lists agree.

Arminian readers take ninety-eight as a real enrollment of this house, not as a symbol.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement, including the added name of Hezekiah attached to Ater in both books.

Both traditions keep the line as a historical count and invent no contrast over a figure that matches.

verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Bezai number three hundred twenty-three; Nehemiah 7:23 has three hundred twenty-four. The two lists should be reported side by side, without choosing one figure as if the other were not written.

Arminian readers take this book’s count as the number it actually records, and they refuse to rewrite it from Nehemiah 7.
verses.reformedNotes:

verses.text: The children of Jorah, one hundred twelve.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Jorah number one hundred twelve. Nehemiah 7:24 has the children of Hariph, one hundred twelve, the same count under a different name. The notes record the difference of name and, where it exists, of number, without forcing one reading.

Arminian readers keep this verse’s wording and refuse to substitute the parallel name as if it had been written here.
verses.reformedNotes:

verses.text: The children of Gibbar, ninety-five.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Gibbar number ninety-five. Nehemiah 7:25 has the children of Gibeon, ninety-five, the same count under a different name. The notes record the difference of name and, where it exists, of number, without forcing one reading.

Arminian readers keep this verse’s wording and refuse to substitute the parallel name as if it had been written here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the two lines side by side. A changed name, and in some cases a changed count, is to be named and left open.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spelling or the figure, and they do not merge the lists.

verses.text: The children of Bethlehem, one hundred twenty-three.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Bethlehem number one hundred twenty-three. The next verse will number the men of Netophah separately, fifty-six. Nehemiah 7:26 combines “The men of Bethlehem and Netophah” at one hundred eighty-eight, which is not the sum of these two lines (one hundred seventy-nine). The different grouping and the different total should both be named.

Arminian readers keep Bethlehem’s own count here and refuse to fold it into the combined Nehemiah figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the separate Bethlehem line unmerged with Netophah, and they report the 188 of Nehemiah 7:26 as a different arrangement, not as a correction of this verse.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the town counts and do not force the two listings into one.

verses.text: The men of Netophah, fifty-six.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Netophah number fifty-six, listed apart from Bethlehem. As already noted, Nehemiah 7:26 joins the two towns at one hundred eighty-eight, while these two verses together come to one hundred seventy-nine. The difference of grouping is part of the larger pattern already in view.

Arminian readers take fifty-six as this book’s count for Netophah, and they do not hide the gap with the combined figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep Netophah distinct here and leave the Nehemiah total unharmonized with the sum of 2:21–22.

Both traditions treat the town lists as records to be compared, not as a puzzle that must be solved in this verse.

verses.text: The men of Anathoth, one hundred twenty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Anathoth number one hundred twenty-eight, the same count as Nehemiah 7:27. Anathoth is a Benjaminite town already known as Jeremiah’s place, though this verse does not retell that history.

Arminian readers take the number as a real enrollment of men from Anathoth in the return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:27 and read the line as a hometown count, not as a symbol drawn from Jeremiah.

Both traditions keep the verse in the list’s ordinary register and invent no contrast over a matching figure.

verses.text: The children of Azmaveth, forty-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Azmaveth number forty-two. Nehemiah 7:28 has the men of Beth Azmaveth at the same figure. The count agrees; the place-name is slightly different and should be reported as such.

Arminian readers take forty-two as the enrollment given here, under the name this verse uses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Azmaveth and Beth Azmaveth side by side, with the same count, and they do not force one form of the name.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the wording and treat the figure as a historical count.

verses.text: The children of Kiriath Arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, seven hundred forty-three.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Kiriath Arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth number seven hundred forty-three, the same total as Nehemiah 7:29, which names Kiriath Jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth. The three Gibeonite towns are grouped together in both lists; only the form Kiriath Arim / Kiriath Jearim differs.

Arminian readers keep WEB’s “Kiriath Arim” here and note the parallel name without rewriting the verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the agreed total and the changed town name, and they refuse to treat the spelling as a doctrinal issue.

Both traditions leave the two forms unharmonized and invent no contrast over them.

verses.text: The children of Ramah and Geba, six hundred twenty-one.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Ramah and Geba number six hundred twenty-one, the same count as Nehemiah 7:30, which speaks of the men of Ramah and Geba. The two Benjaminite towns are grouped together in both lists.

Arminian readers take the joint figure as a real enrollment from these two places.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement in the total, even though one list says children and the other says men.

Both traditions keep the line as a historical count and invent no contrast over the wording.

verses.text: The men of Michmas, one hundred twenty-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Michmas number one hundred twenty-two, the same count as Nehemiah 7:31. The town is listed by itself, and the two books agree on the figure.

Arminian readers take one hundred twenty-two as the enrollment of this place in the return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a matching hometown count and leave the name in its WEB form, Michmas.

Both traditions invent no contrast over a number that agrees, and they do not turn the town into a type.

verses.text: The men of Bethel and Ai, two hundred twenty-three.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Bethel and Ai number two hundred twenty-three. Nehemiah 7:32 has one hundred twenty-three for the same two towns. The counts differ by a hundred and should be left unharmonized.

Arminian readers keep this verse’s two hundred twenty-three and refuse to replace it with the Nehemiah figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name both totals and treat the difference as a fact of the lists, not as a theological problem.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the counts and do not force a single number.

verses.text: The children of Nebo, fifty-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Nebo number fifty-two. Nehemiah 7:33 has the same figure for “The men of the other Nebo”. The count agrees; the wording is not identical, and this list does not use the word other.

Arminian readers take fifty-two as the enrollment given here under the name Nebo, without importing the later wording.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the agreed count and the added word in Nehemiah 7:33, and they leave both lines as they are written.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the name and do not merge the two descriptions.

verses.text: The children of Magbish, one hundred fifty-six.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Magbish number one hundred fifty-six. Nehemiah 7 has no corresponding Magbish line in the parallel town list. The family or place is named only here among the two main lists, and no reason is invented for the silence in Nehemiah.

Arminian readers take one hundred fifty-six as a real enrollment recorded in this book, and they refuse to drop the line in order to match the other list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Magbish as a name peculiar to this chapter in the comparison, without forcing a hidden identification with some other house.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the presence of the line and do not harmonize by omission.

verses.text: The children of the other Elam, one thousand two hundred fifty-four.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of the other Elam number one thousand two hundred fifty-four, the same figure as the Elam of 2:7 and as Nehemiah 7:34. The list itself marks this Elam as the other one, a second house of that name.

Arminian readers take the second Elam as a distinct enrollment, even though the number matches the earlier Elam line.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:34 and the list’s own word other, and they do not collapse the two Elam entries into one house.

Both traditions keep the double entry as the text gives it and invent no contrast over the matching totals.

verses.text: The children of Harim, three hundred twenty.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Harim number three hundred twenty, the same count as Nehemiah 7:35. A priestly house of Harim will appear later, in 2:39, at a different total; this line belongs to the lay list.

Arminian readers take three hundred twenty as the lay enrollment of Harim in the return, not to be confused with the later priestly figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:35 and the distinction between this Harim and the priestly house still to come.

Both traditions keep the count as a historical figure and invent no contrast over a line that matches.

verses.text: The children of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, seven hundred twenty-five.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Lod, Hadid, and Ono number seven hundred twenty-five. Nehemiah 7:37 has seven hundred twenty-one for the same three towns. The two figures should be named and left unharmonized.

Arminian readers keep this verse’s seven hundred twenty-five and do not correct it from the other list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report both totals and treat the difference as a fact of the lists, not as a doctrinal issue.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the four-person gap and refuse to merge the counts.

verses.text: The children of Jericho, three hundred forty-five.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Jericho number three hundred forty-five, the same count as Nehemiah 7:36, though the two books place the Jericho line in a slightly different order among the towns.

Arminian readers take three hundred forty-five as a real enrollment from Jericho in the return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreed total and the different placement in Nehemiah 7, and they do not force the order of the lists into one sequence.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the wording or the shared figure.

verses.text: The children of Senaah, three thousand six hundred thirty.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Senaah number three thousand six hundred thirty, the largest of the lay groups in this unit. Nehemiah 7:38 has three thousand nine hundred thirty for the same name. The counts differ by three hundred and should be left as they stand. The size of the group is not a cue for allegory.

Arminian readers take this book’s three thousand six hundred thirty as the number it records, and they refuse to replace it with the larger Nehemiah figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name both totals and keep the line in the register of the list, a large house, not a symbol.

Both traditions close the lay enrollment without a contrast over the counts, and without forcing the running figures to equal the later assembly total.
